back: Consumer protection agencies include the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). They regulate product safety, labeling and advertising.

front: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing
back: Grades and standards rate products by quality, size or other characteristics, such as USDA grades for meat and eggs. They help customers compare products, give businesses consistent quality measures and support fair pricing.

front: Explain warranties and guarantees
back: A warranty is a promise about a product's quality and what the seller will do if it fails. Express warranties are stated in writing or verbally; implied warranties are automatic under law. A guarantee is a broader promise, often of satisfaction or money back.

front: Explain the nature of product/service branding
back: Branding gives a product or service a name, symbol, design or slogan that identifies it and sets it apart from competitors. Strong brands build recognition, trust and loyalty and allow businesses to charge higher prices.

front: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions
back: A product's life cycle stage affects marketing. In introduction, marketers build awareness; in growth, they expand distribution; in maturity, they differentiate and defend market share; in decline, they cut costs, reposition or discontinue the product.

front: Determine services to provide customers
back: Determining which services to provide customers involves identifying what customers expect and value, such as delivery, installation, returns, credit, repairs or personal assistance, then weighing each service's cost against its benefit to sales and loyalty.

front: Describe the use of technology in the product/service management function
back: Technology in product/service management includes computer-aided design (CAD), 3D printing for prototypes, product lifecycle management software, customer feedback platforms and data analytics that track product performance.

front: Explain business ethics in product/service management
back: Ethics in product/service management involves making safe products, labeling honestly, not exaggerating benefits, avoiding planned obsolescence that harms customers, recalling defective products promptly and respecting others' intellectual property.

front: Describe the nature of product bundling
back: Product bundling combines two or more products or services into one package sold at a single price, often lower than buying them separately. Examples include hotel-and-flight vacation packages or meal combos. Bundling increases sales and adds value for customers.

front: Describe factors used by marketers to position products/services
back: Marketers position products based on factors such as features and benefits, price and quality, use or application, target user, comparison with competitors and the product's category. The goal is a clear, favorable place in customers' minds.

front: Calculate open-to-buy
back: Open-to-buy (OTB) is the amount of merchandise a buyer can still purchase for a period without exceeding the budget. OTB = planned purchases − merchandise already on order. It helps prevent overbuying.

front: Explain the nature of merchandise plans (budgets)
back: A merchandise plan (budget) forecasts sales, stock levels, reductions and purchases for a period, usually by month and department. It guides buying decisions so retailers have the right amount of stock to meet sales goals.

front: Plan stock
back: Planning stock means determining how much inventory is needed at the beginning of each period to meet planned sales. Buyers use methods such as the stock-to-sales ratio and consider seasonality and turnover goals.

front: Plan reductions (e.g., anticipated markdowns, employee/other discounts, stock shortages)
back: Planning reductions means estimating decreases in inventory value from markdowns, employee and other discounts and stock shortages (shrinkage). Planned reductions are included in the merchandise budget to calculate purchases.

front: Plan purchases
back: Planned purchases = planned sales + planned reductions + planned ending inventory − planned beginning inventory. This shows how much merchandise a buyer should purchase for a period.

front: Explain the concept of product in the hospitality and tourism industry
back: The product in hospitality and tourism is mostly an experience, such as lodging, meals, transportation, attractions and service. It combines tangible elements (room, food) with intangible ones (atmosphere, staff friendliness) that shape guest satisfaction.

front: Explain the nature of product extension in services marketing
back: Product extension in services marketing means adding new services under an existing brand or expanding current services, such as a gym adding online classes. It uses the brand's reputation to attract customers to the new offering.

front: Explain the concept of “product” in marketing communications
back: In marketing communications, the 'product' is the service the agency or department provides, such as advertising campaigns, PR, social media management or content, along with the ideas, creativity and expertise behind it.

front: Describe services offered by the hospitality and tourism industry
back: The hospitality and tourism industry offers lodging, food and beverage, transportation, travel planning, attractions and entertainment, recreation, and meetings and events. Many businesses combine these, such as resorts offering rooms, dining and activities.

front: Explain the nature of product extensions in the hospitality and tourism industry
back: Product extensions in hospitality and tourism add new offerings under an existing brand, such as a hotel chain launching a budget or extended-stay brand, a restaurant selling packaged sauces or a theme park adding a water park. Extensions use brand recognition to attract customers.

front: Build corporate brands
back: A corporate brand represents the entire company rather than one product. Building it involves defining the company's values and promise, using a consistent name, logo and message, delivering quality experiences and engaging in socially responsible activities.

front: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea
back: Techniques for generating product ideas include brainstorming, customer surveys and feedback, studying competitors, observing customer problems, trend research, employee suggestions, SCAMPER and partnerships with suppliers or universities.

front: Generate product ideas
back: Generating product ideas means coming up with many possible new products or improvements. Teams use brainstorming, customer insights, trends and problem-solving, then screen ideas for feasibility and fit with the company.

front: Determine initial feasibility of product idea
back: Determining initial feasibility of a product idea means quickly checking whether it is worth developing further. Questions include: Is there demand? Can it be made at a reasonable cost? Does it fit the company? Are there legal or technical barriers?

front: Identify product opportunities
back: Identifying product opportunities means finding unmet customer needs, gaps in competitors' offerings, emerging trends, new technologies and ways to improve existing products that could lead to new products.

front: Create processes for ongoing opportunity recognition
back: Processes for ongoing opportunity recognition help a business keep finding new product ideas. They include gathering customer feedback, monitoring trends and competitors, encouraging employee suggestions and reviewing sales data for gaps and unmet needs.

front: Evaluate customer experience
back: Evaluating customer experience means measuring how customers feel about every interaction with a business. Methods include satisfaction surveys, Net Promoter Score, reviews, mystery shoppers and customer journey mapping. Results show where to improve.

front: Generate marketing communications ideas
back: Generating marketing communications ideas involves understanding the client's goals and audience, researching, brainstorming, building on insights, sketching concepts and testing ideas against the brief to find the most effective approach.

front: Compare and contrast buying from domestic sources with that of foreign sources
back: Buying from domestic sources offers faster delivery, easier communication, fewer regulations and lower shipping risk. Foreign sources may offer lower prices and unique products but involve longer lead times, tariffs, currency risk and quality-control challenges.

front: Determine final cost of purchases from domestic and international sources
back: The final (landed) cost of purchases includes the product price plus shipping, insurance, duties and tariffs, customs fees, currency exchange costs and handling. International purchases often cost much more than the quoted price.

front: Adjust idea to create functional product
back: Adjusting an idea to create a functional product means refining a concept so it works in real use and can be produced. This involves prototyping, testing, gathering feedback, fixing design flaws and balancing features with cost.

front: Explain the nature of corporate branding
back: Corporate branding promotes the company as a whole rather than individual products. It builds a reputation based on the company's values, quality and image, which strengthens all of its products and builds trust with customers, employees and investors.

front: Describe factors used by businesses to position corporate brands
back: Factors used to position a corporate brand include the company's values and mission, quality reputation, innovation, customer service, social responsibility, heritage and the image the company wants to project compared with competitors.

front: Build product/service brand
back: Building a product or service brand means creating a distinct identity that customers recognize and trust. It involves choosing a name, logo and slogan, defining the brand's promise, communicating it consistently and delivering quality that supports it.

front: Assess product-packaging requirements
back: Assessing packaging requirements means determining what packaging must do: protect the product, meet legal labeling rules, fit shipping and shelf needs, attract buyers, communicate information and meet cost and sustainability goals.

front: Communicate core values of product/service
back: Communicating a product's core values means expressing what the brand stands for, such as quality, sustainability or family fun, through consistent messages, design, employee behavior and customer experience.

front: Create/maintain daily sales plan
back: A daily sales plan sets sales goals for each day based on past sales, events, promotions and seasonal patterns. Managers track actual sales against it and adjust staffing and activities to meet goals.

front: Describe services offered by the marketing-communications industry
back: The marketing communications industry offers advertising, public relations, digital and social media marketing, content creation, media planning and buying, branding, event marketing, direct marketing and market research.

front: Determine quality of merchandise to offer
back: Determining the quality of merchandise to offer depends on the target market, store image, price points, competition and customer expectations. A discount store and a luxury boutique offer very different quality levels.

front: Determine stock turnover
back: Stock turnover shows how many times inventory is sold and replaced during a period. Turnover = net sales ÷ average inventory at retail (or COGS ÷ average inventory at cost). Higher turnover usually means fresher stock and better cash flow.

front: Develop positioning concept for a new product idea
back: A positioning concept describes how a new product should be perceived compared with competitors. It identifies the target market, the product's main benefit or point of difference and the reason customers should believe it.

front: Establish reorder points
back: A reorder point is the inventory level at which more stock should be ordered. Reorder point = (daily sales × lead time in days) + safety stock. It prevents running out while waiting for deliveries.

front: Evaluate adequacy of product packaging
back: Evaluating packaging adequacy means checking whether a package protects the product, is convenient to use, meets labeling laws, stands out on the shelf, communicates the brand and is cost-effective and environmentally responsible.

front: Evaluate graphic design on packages
back: Evaluating package graphic design means judging whether colors, fonts, images and layout attract attention, communicate the brand and key benefits, are easy to read, appeal to the target market and stand out from competitors.

front: Evaluate vendors' goods and services
back: Evaluating vendors' goods and services means comparing suppliers on quality, price, reliability, delivery time, service, payment terms and reputation. Businesses may use samples, references and scorecards to choose the best vendor.

front: Explain new product-development processes
back: New product development typically follows these steps: idea generation, idea screening, concept development and testing, business analysis, product development, test marketing and commercialization (launch).

front: Identify components of a retail image
back: Components of a retail image include merchandise, prices, store design and layout, atmosphere (lighting, music, displays), location, customer service, advertising and the types of customers the store attracts.

front: Identify product's/service's competitive advantage
back: A competitive advantage is what makes a product or service better than competitors' in customers' eyes, such as lower price, higher quality, better location, unique features or superior service. Identifying it helps focus marketing.

front: Obtain samples
back: Obtaining samples means requesting examples of products from vendors to check quality, fit, materials and appeal before placing large orders. Samples help buyers make better decisions and avoid costly mistakes.

front: Plan merchandise assortment (e.g., styling, sizes, quantities, colors)
back: Planning a merchandise assortment means deciding the mix of styles, sizes, colors and quantities to carry. Buyers consider sales history, customer preferences, trends, budget and store space to balance breadth and depth.

front: Identify emerging trends
back: Identifying emerging trends means spotting new styles, products and consumer preferences early by watching fashion shows, social media, influencers, trade shows, sales data and competitors.

front: Write purchase orders
back: Writing a purchase order means creating a document that lists the vendor, items, descriptions, quantities, prices, delivery dates, shipping instructions and payment terms. Once accepted, it becomes a binding agreement.

front: Analyze the use of central buying
back: Central buying means a retail chain's headquarters buys merchandise for all stores. Advantages include volume discounts, consistent assortments and expert buyers. Disadvantages include less flexibility for local tastes and slower response.

front: Determine what to buy/reorder
back: Determining what to buy or reorder means analyzing sales data, inventory levels, customer requests, trends and the merchandise plan to choose items that will sell well and fit the store's image.

front: Determine quantities to buy/reorder
back: Determining quantities to buy means balancing expected sales with inventory goals, considering sales history, open-to-buy, minimum order quantities, lead times, discounts and storage space.

front: Determine when to buy/reorder
back: Determining when to buy means timing orders so merchandise arrives before demand, based on seasons, lead times, reorder points, promotions and vendor schedules.

front: Choose vendors
back: Choosing vendors means selecting suppliers based on product quality, price, reliability, delivery speed, terms of sale, reputation, service and how well their products fit the store's assortment and image.

front: Negotiate terms with suppliers
back: Negotiating terms with suppliers means discussing price, discounts, payment terms, shipping costs, delivery dates, return privileges and advertising allowances to get the best overall value.

front: Identify company's unique selling proposition
back: A unique selling proposition (USP) is the specific benefit that sets a business or product apart from competitors, such as lowest price, fastest delivery or best quality. Identifying it requires knowing customer needs and competitors' offerings.

front: Identify internal and external service standards
back: Service standards define the level of service a business promises. Internal standards set expectations for how employees serve each other, such as response times between departments. External standards set expectations for customers, such as wait times or return policies.

front: Establish credibility with Internet users
back: Establishing credibility with internet users means having a professional, secure website; providing accurate, useful content; showing reviews and testimonials; displaying contact information; being transparent about the business; and responding to users.

front: Identify opportunities in the social-media space
back: Identifying social media opportunities means finding ways to use social platforms for business goals, such as reaching new audiences, engaging customers, selling directly, partnering with influencers or using new platform features.

front: Describe the role of customer voice in branding
back: Customer voice, meaning reviews, social media posts, testimonials and word of mouth, shapes how a brand is perceived. Brands listen to and engage with customers, use feedback to improve and share positive stories to build trust.

front: Identify customer touch points
back: Customer touch points are every place a customer interacts with a brand, including ads, the website, social media, the store, salespeople, packaging, customer service and follow-up emails. Each touch point shapes the customer's perception of the brand.

front: Determine the impact of product standards' issues associated with global business
back: Product standards differ across countries, covering safety, labeling, measurements, electrical requirements and environmental rules. Global businesses must adapt products to meet each market's standards, which affects cost and time to market.

front: Describe the uses of grades and standards in lodging
back: Grades and standards in lodging, such as star ratings (Forbes Travel Guide) and diamond ratings (AAA), classify properties by quality, service and amenities. They help guests compare properties and help hotels set and maintain standards.

front: Explain the role of guest services
back: Guest services help guests enjoy their stay by handling requests and providing information and assistance. They include bell services, concierge, transportation, wake-up calls and luggage storage, and they directly shape guest satisfaction.

front: Discuss the nature of concierge services
back: Concierge services assist guests with special requests, such as restaurant reservations, tickets to shows, transportation, tours and local recommendations. Concierges build local connections to deliver personalized experiences.

front: Describe the purpose of guest relations
back: Guest relations focus on building positive relationships with guests by welcoming VIPs, handling special occasions, resolving complaints, gathering feedback and creating personalized experiences that build loyalty.

front: Describe the uses of grades and standards in foodservice
back: Grades and standards in foodservice, such as USDA grades for beef (Prime, Choice, Select), eggs and produce, indicate quality. They help buyers specify exactly what they want, compare suppliers and maintain consistent menu quality.

front: Determine effect of changes in nutritional guidelines
back: Changes in nutritional guidelines, such as new dietary recommendations or labeling rules, can lead restaurants to adjust recipes, portion sizes and menu options, add nutritional information and market healthier choices.

front: Discuss the nature of the menu as a management tool
back: The menu is a management tool because it determines what ingredients to buy, what equipment and skills are needed, staffing, kitchen layout, pricing and profitability. It is also a key marketing tool that influences what guests order.

front: Describe foodservice branding strategies (e.g., retail-item, restaurant, in-house/signature, branded concept)
back: Foodservice branding strategies include retail-item branding (selling packaged products), restaurant branding (building the restaurant's own identity), in-house or signature items (unique dishes) and branded concepts (offering a known brand, such as a coffee chain inside a hotel).

front: Explain guarantees in hospitality and tourism
back: Guarantees in hospitality and tourism promise guests a certain level of service or a remedy if it isn't met, such as a satisfaction guarantee, price-match promise or 'on-time or it's free' pledge. They reduce guests' risk and show confidence in service quality.

front: Describe the role of customer voice in hospitality and tourism branding
back: Customer voice, meaning what guests say through reviews, social media and feedback, shapes hospitality brands. Positive word of mouth builds credibility, while complaints can damage the brand. Businesses monitor and respond to customer voice to strengthen their image.

front: Choose hospitality and tourism vendors
back: Choosing hospitality and tourism vendors involves identifying needs (food, linens, equipment, technology), comparing suppliers on quality, price, reliability and service, checking references and selecting vendors who support consistent guest experiences.

front: Negotiate terms with hospitality and tourism suppliers
back: Negotiating with suppliers means discussing price, quantity, quality, delivery schedules, payment terms and contract length to reach an agreement that benefits both sides. Good negotiators prepare, know alternatives and build long-term relationships.

front: Explain the role of promotion as a marketing function
back: Promotion is the marketing function that communicates with customers to inform, persuade and remind them about products, services, images or ideas. It builds awareness, encourages purchases and supports the company's image.

front: Explain the types of promotion (i.e., institutional, product)
back: Product promotion focuses on selling specific goods or services. Institutional promotion builds the company's image, goodwill and reputation rather than promoting a specific product, for example a company highlighting its community involvement.

front: Identify the elements of the promotional mix
back: The promotional mix is the combination of promotional elements a business uses: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations and direct marketing (many also include digital and social media). Businesses blend these to reach their goals.

front: Explain types of advertising media
back: Advertising media include print (newspapers, magazines), broadcast (TV, radio), digital (websites, social media, search, streaming), out-of-home (billboards, transit) and direct mail. Each differs in cost, reach, targeting and the type of message it suits.

front: Calculate media costs
back: Media costs are often compared using cost per thousand (CPM): ad cost ÷ (audience size ÷ 1,000). For example, a $5,000 ad reaching 250,000 people has a CPM of $20. Digital ads may also be priced per click (CPC) or per action.

front: Explain the components of advertisements
back: The main components of an advertisement are the headline (grabs attention), copy (the message and details), illustration (images or graphics), signature (logo, company name, contact information) and often a slogan and call to action.

front: Explain the use of visual merchandising in retailing
back: Visual merchandising is the presentation of a store and its merchandise to attract customers and encourage purchases. It includes the storefront, layout, displays, signage, lighting and color, and it communicates the store's image.

front: Explain types of display arrangements
back: Types of display arrangements include pyramid (triangular, building to a peak), step (rising like stairs), zigzag (a varied pyramid), radiation (lines extending from a central point) and repetition (the same items repeated in a row).

front: Select and use display fixtures/forms
back: Selecting display fixtures and forms means choosing equipment, such as mannequins, racks, shelves, tables, gondolas and risers, that suits the merchandise, shows it at its best, fits the space and matches the store's image.

front: Create displays
back: Creating a display involves choosing a theme and merchandise, selecting fixtures and props, using an arrangement pattern, applying color, balance and a focal point, adding lighting and signs and checking it from the customer's view.

front: Maintain displays
back: Maintaining displays means keeping them clean, fully stocked, neat and in working order. Staff replace sold or damaged items, straighten merchandise, fix lighting and update signs and prices.

front: Dismantle/Store displays/display fixtures/forms
back: Dismantling a display means removing merchandise and returning it to stock, carefully taking apart fixtures and props, cleaning and labeling them and storing them safely so they can be reused.

front: Analyze costs/benefits of company participation in community activities
back: Analyzing costs and benefits of community activities means comparing what participation costs (money, time, products, staff) with its benefits (goodwill, publicity, employee morale, customer loyalty and community relationships).

front: Write a press release
back: A press release announces newsworthy information to the media. It includes a headline, dateline, a lead paragraph answering who, what, when, where and why, supporting details and quotes, a boilerplate about the company and contact information.

front: Prepare store/department for special event
back: Preparing a store for a special event includes setting up displays and signs, arranging merchandise, decorating, preparing equipment, briefing staff on their roles and making sure the store is clean, safe and ready for crowds.

front: Explain the nature of a promotional plan
back: A promotional plan is a written plan for using promotion to reach marketing goals. It includes objectives, target audience, budget, the promotional mix, messages, schedule and how results will be measured.

front: Coordinate activities in the promotional mix
back: Coordinating the promotional mix means making advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, PR and direct and digital marketing work together with a consistent message and timing, called integrated marketing communications.

front: Plan/Schedule displays/themes with management
back: Planning displays with management means agreeing on themes, timing, merchandise to feature, budget and locations so displays support promotions, seasons and sales goals across the store.

front: Explain the use of advertising agencies
back: Advertising agencies create, plan and place advertising for clients. Businesses use them for creative expertise, media buying power, research and strategy. Agencies may be full-service or specialize in areas such as digital or media buying.

front: Explain promotional methods used by the hospitality and tourism industry
back: Hospitality and tourism promotional methods include advertising, social media and influencer marketing, websites and email, loyalty programs, special packages and discounts, public relations, travel shows and partnerships with travel agents and online booking sites.

front: Explain the nature of direct marketing channels
back: Direct marketing channels communicate directly with individual customers to get a response. Examples include direct mail, email, telemarketing, text messages, catalogs and direct-response TV. They allow personalization and make results easy to measure.

front: Describe the use of business ethics in promotion
back: Ethics in promotion means communicating honestly and responsibly. Ethical promoters avoid false or exaggerated claims, hidden terms, offensive content and manipulative tactics aimed at vulnerable groups such as children, and they disclose paid endorsements.

front: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function
back: Technology in promotion includes social media platforms, search engine marketing, programmatic advertising, email automation, mobile and location-based ads, analytics tools that measure results and design software for creating ads.

front: Describe the regulation of promotion
back: Promotion is regulated mainly by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), which prohibits deceptive and unfair advertising and requires disclosure of endorsements. Other rules include the FCC for broadcast, CAN-SPAM for email, the Do Not Call Registry and FDA rules for food and drug ads.

front: Buy ad space/time
back: Buying ad space or time means selecting media, negotiating rates, choosing placement and schedule, signing insertion orders or contracts and confirming that ads run as agreed. Media buyers aim to reach the target audience at the lowest cost.

front: Create promotional signs
back: Creating promotional signs means writing a short, clear message, including the price or offer, using readable fonts and strong contrast, matching store branding and placing the sign where customers will see it.

front: Set up point-of-sale displays and handouts
back: Setting up point-of-sale displays means placing promotional displays, signs and handouts near the register or product location to encourage impulse purchases and inform customers about offers.

front: Explain considerations affecting global promotion
back: Global promotion must consider language and translation, cultural values and symbols, laws and regulations, media availability, local competition and whether to standardize messages worldwide or adapt them to each market.

front: Describe the concept of promotion in the hospitality and tourism industry
back: Promotion in hospitality and tourism communicates the experience a guest can expect, since the service can't be seen before purchase. It uses images, reviews and stories to inform, persuade and remind potential guests to book or visit.

front: Write direct-mail letters
back: Writing direct-mail letters means personalizing the greeting, opening with a strong attention-getter, explaining benefits, providing proof, making a clear offer and ending with a call to action. A P.S. often restates the offer.

front: Describe the use of color in advertisements
back: Color in advertisements attracts attention, creates mood and reinforces brand identity. For example, red suggests excitement, blue suggests trust and green suggests health or nature. Colors must be readable and consistent with the brand.

front: Describe the nature of copy strategies
back: A copy strategy defines what an ad's words should accomplish: the target audience, the main benefit or promise, the support for that promise and the tone or style. It guides copywriters so messages stay focused and consistent.

front: Check advertising proofs
back: Checking advertising proofs means reviewing an ad before it runs for errors in spelling, prices, dates, contact information, images and layout, and confirming it meets the client's approval and media requirements.

front: Schedule ads and commercials
back: Scheduling ads and commercials means deciding when and how often they run. Patterns include continuous (steady), flighting (bursts with gaps) and pulsing (steady with bursts). Schedules match seasons, sales periods and audience habits.

front: Select placement of advertisements
back: Selecting ad placement means choosing where an ad appears, such as page position, TV program, time slot, website or social feed. Good placement reaches the target audience when they are most attentive.

front: Explain the nature of online advertising (e.g., email, search, social media, display, mobile)
back: Online advertising includes email ads and newsletters, search ads (paid results on search engines), social media ads, display ads (banners and video on websites) and mobile ads. It offers precise targeting and measurable results.

front: Explain the nature of email marketing tactics
back: Email marketing tactics include newsletters, promotional offers, welcome series, abandoned-cart reminders, personalized recommendations and re-engagement emails. Effective emails have strong subject lines, clear calls to action, mobile-friendly design and permission-based lists.

front: Execute targeted emails
back: Executing targeted emails means segmenting the email list, personalizing content, writing strong subject lines, testing versions, sending at the best time, complying with CAN-SPAM and tracking opens, clicks and conversions.

front: Cultivate media relationships
back: Cultivating media relationships means building trust with journalists and editors. PR professionals provide accurate, timely and newsworthy information, respect deadlines, are available for interviews and tailor stories to each outlet's audience.

front: Develop promotional calendar
back: A promotional calendar schedules all promotions, events, ads and displays for the year. It aligns with holidays, seasons and merchandise plans and helps coordinate advertising, buying and staffing.

front: Describe the elements of design
back: The elements of design are line, shape, color, texture, value (lightness or darkness), space and typography. Designers combine them using principles such as balance, contrast, emphasis and unity to create attractive, effective promotions.

front: Determine advertising reach of media
back: Advertising reach is the number or percentage of the target audience exposed to an ad at least once during a period. Frequency is how many times they see it. Media planners use audience data to estimate reach and balance it with frequency and cost.

front: Create a press kit
back: A press kit gives journalists information about a company or event. It typically includes press releases, a company fact sheet and background, executive biographies, photos and logos, recent coverage and contact information.

front: Identify techniques to increase ad response time
back: Techniques to increase ad response include strong calls to action, limited-time offers, clear benefits, easy response methods (QR codes, links, phone numbers), incentives and targeting the right audience at the right time.

front: Collaborate in the design of collateral materials to promote frequency/loyalty marketing program
back: Designing collateral for a loyalty program involves creating cards, brochures, signs, emails and app screens that explain how to join, earn and redeem rewards, using consistent branding and clear benefits.

front: Participate in the design of collateral materials to promote special events
back: Collateral materials for special events include flyers, posters, invitations, brochures, banners, programs, signage and social media graphics. Designing them involves matching the event's theme and brand, including key details and making materials eye-catching and clear.

front: Set up cross-promotions
back: Cross-promotion is when two or more businesses promote each other's products, such as a movie partnering with a fast-food chain. Setting it up involves finding a compatible partner, agreeing on goals and terms and coordinating materials.

front: Participate in trade shows/expositions
back: Participating in a trade show involves planning goals, designing an attractive booth, preparing materials and demonstrations, training staff, engaging visitors, collecting leads and following up after the show.

front: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences
back: Word-of-mouth channels spread messages through people talking to each other. They include personal recommendations, online reviews, social media sharing, referral programs, influencers and brand ambassadors. Because they come from peers, they are highly trusted.

front: Identify communications channels used in sales promotion
back: Sales promotion channels deliver short-term incentives to buy. They include in-store displays and signage, coupons in print or apps, email and text offers, social media contests, loyalty programs, samples and trade shows.

front: Explain communications channels used in public-relations activities
back: Public-relations channels include news releases, press conferences, media interviews, company websites and blogs, social media, newsletters, speeches, sponsorships and community events. They earn publicity and build goodwill rather than paying for ad space.

front: Explain the importance of coordinating elements in advertisements
back: Coordinating the elements of an ad means making the headline, copy, illustration and signature work together to deliver one clear message. Consistent layout, color and tone attract attention, make the ad easy to read and strengthen brand recognition.

front: Identify types of public-relations activities
back: Public-relations activities include writing news releases, holding press conferences, sponsoring events, participating in community service, publishing newsletters, handling crises and managing relationships with media, investors and the public.

front: Discuss internal and external audiences for public-relations activities
back: Public-relations audiences can be internal (employees, managers, shareholders) or external (customers, media, community, suppliers, government, investors). PR professionals tailor messages and channels to each audience's interests.

front: Explain how businesses can use trade-show/exposition participation to communicate with targeted audiences
back: Trade shows let businesses meet targeted audiences face to face, demonstrate products, launch new offerings, gather leads, meet distributors and media and learn about competitors and industry trends.

front: Explain considerations used to evaluate whether to participate in trade shows/expositions
back: Deciding whether to attend a trade show means considering cost (booth, travel, materials), attendee profile and size, fit with target market, competitors' presence, goals and expected return on investment.

front: Collaborate in the design of slogans/taglines
back: A slogan or tagline is a short, memorable phrase that expresses a brand's personality or main benefit. Designing one involves understanding the brand, brainstorming, keeping it short and easy to remember and testing it with the audience.

front: Create a public-service announcement
back: A public-service announcement (PSA) is a noncommercial message that informs or encourages action on a public issue, such as safety or health. Creating one means choosing a clear message, target audience, emotional appeal and call to action.

front: Create written briefs for outside agencies/consultants
back: A written brief tells an outside agency or consultant what is needed. It includes background, objectives, target audience, key message, deliverables, budget, timeline and how success will be measured.

front: Describe considerations in developing customer evangelists
back: Customer evangelists are loyal customers who actively recommend a brand. Developing them involves delivering excellent experiences, listening to and involving customers, rewarding advocacy, building community and making it easy to share.

front: Describe digital color concepts
back: Digital color concepts include the RGB color model (red, green and blue light) used for screens, hexadecimal codes for web colors and resolution. Print uses CMYK instead, so colors must be converted for consistent results.

front: Describe effective advertising layouts
back: Effective advertising layouts arrange the headline, illustration, copy and signature so the eye moves naturally through the ad. They use a clear focal point, balance, white space and a logical flow ending with the call to action.

front: Describe mobile marketing tactics
back: Mobile marketing tactics include SMS and MMS messages, push notifications, mobile apps, mobile-optimized websites and ads, QR codes, location-based offers and in-app advertising. They reach customers wherever they are.

front: Describe referral programs that can be used to build brand/promote products
back: Referral programs reward customers for recommending a business, often with discounts, credits or gifts for both the referrer and the new customer. They spread word of mouth and attract new customers at low cost.

front: Describe the nature of effective Internet ad copy
back: Effective internet ad copy is short, clear and benefit-focused, uses relevant keywords, includes a strong call to action and matches the landing page. It must grab attention quickly because users scroll fast.

front: Describe the use of blogging for marketing communications
back: Blogging lets businesses share useful content, show expertise, improve search engine ranking and build relationships with customers. Effective business blogs post regularly, target audience interests and include calls to action.

front: Describe the use of crisis management in public relations
back: Crisis management in PR means preparing for and responding to events that threaten a company's reputation. It involves having a plan, responding quickly and honestly, using a single spokesperson, showing concern and keeping stakeholders informed.

front: Determine on-floor assortments
back: Determining on-floor assortments means deciding which items, sizes, colors and quantities to place on the sales floor, based on sales, space, season and promotions, while keeping backup stock in the stockroom.

front: Discuss the nature of effective direct-mail copy
back: Effective direct-mail copy is personal, clear and benefit-focused. It uses an attention-grabbing headline, addresses the reader's needs, includes proof such as testimonials, presents a clear offer and ends with an easy call to action.

front: Discuss the nature of typography
back: Typography is the style and arrangement of text, including typeface, size, spacing and alignment. Good typography makes ads readable, sets a tone (formal, playful, modern) and supports the brand identity.

front: Discuss the use of marketing/creative briefs
back: A marketing or creative brief is a short document that guides a creative team. It describes the project's objective, target audience, key message, tone, deliverables, budget and deadlines, keeping everyone aligned.

front: Discuss the use of podcasts/webcasts
back: Podcasts are audio or video shows people can download or stream; webcasts are live or recorded online broadcasts. Businesses use them to share expertise, build relationships, reach niche audiences and promote products.

front: Discuss the use of search engine optimization tactics for digital marketing
back: Search engine optimization (SEO) tactics help a website rank higher in unpaid search results. They include using relevant keywords, quality content, fast and mobile-friendly pages, clear titles and descriptions and earning links from other reputable sites.

front: Discuss the use of social bookmarking/tagging
back: Social bookmarking and tagging let users save, organize and share web content with labels (tags) and hashtags. Marketers use them to make content easier to discover and to track what topics their audience follows.

front: Discuss types of direct mail tactics
back: Direct mail tactics include postcards, letters, catalogs, brochures, coupons and samples sent to targeted mailing lists. Personalization, a clear offer and a call to action improve response rates, which are easy to track.

front: Distinguish between visual merchandising and display
back: Visual merchandising covers the entire store's presentation, including layout, fixtures, signage, lighting and atmosphere. Display is one part of it: the specific arrangement of merchandise to attract attention in a window or on the floor.

front: Explain considerations in developing viral marketing campaigns
back: Viral marketing campaigns are designed to be shared widely by people online. Considerations include creating emotional, entertaining or useful content, making it easy to share, timing, platform fit, brand relevance and the risk of negative reactions.

front: Explain current issues/trends in public relations
back: Current public relations trends include social media and influencer relations, rapid crisis response, brand purpose and social responsibility, data-driven PR measurement, owned media content and fighting misinformation.

front: Explain the impact of color harmonies on composition
back: Color harmonies are pleasing combinations, such as complementary (opposites on the color wheel), analogous (neighbors) and monochromatic (shades of one color). Harmonies create balance, guide attention and set mood in a composition.

front: Explain the importance of company involvement in community activities
back: Company involvement in community activities builds goodwill, strengthens the company's reputation, improves employee morale, creates positive publicity and builds relationships with customers and local leaders.

front: Explain the marketing-communications development process
back: The marketing communications development process includes researching the situation and audience, setting objectives, developing strategy and creative concepts, producing materials, launching the campaign and measuring results.

front: Explain the nature of buzz-marketing
back: Buzz marketing creates excitement and conversation around a product, often through unusual events, teasers, exclusive previews, influencers or viral content. The goal is for people to talk about and share the brand on their own.

front: Explain the nature of effective mobile ad copy
back: Effective mobile ad copy is very short, clear and action-oriented, with the key message up front, a simple call to action (tap, call, download) and design that fits small screens and quick attention spans.

front: Explain the nature of word-of-mouth (WOM) strategies
back: Word-of-mouth strategies encourage customers to recommend a business. They include referral programs, encouraging reviews, loyalty rewards, brand ambassadors, shareable experiences and excellent service that people want to talk about.

front: Explain the use of celebrities/influencers as a WOM strategy
back: Celebrities and influencers promote products to their followers, who trust their opinions. This word-of-mouth strategy builds awareness and credibility, but the influencer must fit the brand and paid endorsements must be disclosed.

front: Explain the use of illustrations in advertisements
back: Illustrations in advertisements, such as photos, drawings and graphics, attract attention, show the product in use, create emotional appeal and communicate quickly. They should be relevant to the message and the target audience.

front: Explain the use of product placement
back: Product placement is paying to have a product shown or used in movies, TV shows, video games or online videos. It exposes the product naturally to viewers without a traditional ad.

front: Explain the use of RSS feeds
back: RSS feeds deliver updated website content, such as blog posts, news or podcasts, to subscribers automatically through feed readers. Businesses use them to keep audiences informed and drive traffic back to their sites.

front: Explain type styles used in advertisements
back: Type styles used in advertisements include serif (traditional, formal), sans serif (clean, modern), script (elegant, personal) and decorative (attention-grabbing). Advertisers often use one style for headlines and another for body copy, keeping text easy to read.

front: Explain website-development process
back: The website development process includes planning (goals and audience), designing (layout and branding), creating content, developing and coding, testing on devices and browsers, launching and maintaining and updating the site.

front: Identify effective advertising headlines
back: Effective advertising headlines grab attention, highlight a benefit, appeal to the target audience and encourage reading the rest of the ad. They may ask a question, make a promise, offer news or use a command.

front: Identify strategies for attracting targeted audience to website
back: Strategies for attracting a target audience to a website include SEO, paid search ads, social media posts, email marketing, content marketing, links from partner sites and promoting the URL on packaging, ads and signs.

front: Identify types of drawing media
back: Drawing media are materials used to create illustrations, including pencil, charcoal, ink, markers, pastels, watercolor and digital drawing tools such as tablets and software. Each produces a different look and feel.

front: Identify ways to track marketing-communications activities
back: Ways to track marketing communications activities include project management tools, content calendars, analytics dashboards, media monitoring, campaign codes and tracking links, and regular status reports.

front: Negotiate terms with media owner
back: Negotiating with media owners means discussing ad rates, placement, frequency, bonuses (such as extra spots), deadlines and payment terms to get the best value. Buying larger packages or long-term commitments can earn discounts.

front: Participate in community outreach activities
back: Participating in community outreach means representing the business in community activities, such as volunteering, sponsoring local events or supporting charities. It builds goodwill, relationships and a positive company image.

front: Place merchandise for impact
back: Placing merchandise for impact means putting high-demand, new or promoted items in high-traffic areas, at eye level, near entrances, on endcaps and near registers so customers see them and are more likely to buy.

front: Proof ads
back: Proofing ads means carefully checking ads before they run for errors in prices, dates, product names, images, spelling and contact information, and confirming they match the approved plan.

front: Propose community issues for company involvement
back: Proposing community issues for involvement means identifying causes that matter to the community and align with the company's values and customers, such as education or the environment, and recommending how the company can help.

front: Read media schedule
back: A media schedule shows when and where ads will run, including media outlets, dates, times or placements, frequency and costs. Reading it means understanding the plan and checking that ads run as scheduled.

front: Read/Implement planograms
back: A planogram is a diagram showing exactly where and how each product should be placed on a shelf or fixture. Implementing it means setting merchandise as shown so stores are consistent and space is used to maximize sales.

front: Use cross-merchandising techniques
back: Cross-merchandising means displaying related products from different categories together, such as chips next to salsa or belts with pants, to encourage customers to buy additional items.

front: Use lighting to highlight products
back: Lighting highlights products by drawing attention, creating mood and showing true colors. Retailers use spotlights on featured items, bright general lighting for shopping and warm or cool tones to fit the merchandise.

front: Plan special events
back: Planning a special event, such as a sale, product launch or in-store demonstration, involves setting goals, choosing a date and theme, budgeting, promoting the event, preparing merchandise and staff and evaluating results afterward.

front: Write email marketing copy
back: Writing email marketing copy means crafting a compelling subject line and preview text, personalizing the message, keeping it short and scannable, focusing on benefits and including one clear call-to-action button.

front: Discuss the role of customer voice in word-of-mouth strategies
back: Customer voice, meaning reviews, testimonials and social media posts, powers word-of-mouth strategies because people trust other customers more than ads. Businesses encourage, share and respond to customer voice to spread positive messages.

front: Explain the role of business websites in digital marketing
back: A business website is the center of digital marketing. It provides information, sells products, captures leads, supports SEO and content marketing, and is where ads, social media and email campaigns usually direct customers.

front: Explain the use of social media for digital marketing
back: Social media is used in digital marketing to build brand awareness, engage customers, share content, run targeted ads, provide customer service and drive website traffic. Each platform suits different audiences and types of content.

front: Explain the use of video/images for digital marketing
back: Video and images in digital marketing capture attention quickly, show products in action, tell brand stories and are widely shared. Short videos, high-quality photos and live streams increase engagement on websites and social media.

front: Explain mobile marketing applications
back: Mobile marketing applications include branded apps, loyalty and rewards apps, mobile ordering and payment, mobile coupons, push notifications and augmented reality features. Apps keep the brand on customers' phones and provide useful data.

front: Write copy for advertisements
back: Writing ad copy means creating a headline that grabs attention, body copy that explains benefits and gives reasons to buy, and a call to action, all in a tone that fits the brand and target audience.

front: Write content for use on the website
back: Writing website content means creating clear, scannable text with headings and bullet points, focusing on visitors' needs, using keywords for SEO, keeping the brand voice consistent and guiding visitors toward an action.

front: Write content for use in social media
back: Writing social media content means creating short, engaging posts suited to each platform, using an authentic brand voice, adding visuals and hashtags, encouraging interaction and posting consistently.

front: Write mobile marketing content
back: Writing mobile marketing content means keeping messages brief and direct, putting the most important information first, using clear calls to action and making sure links and offers work well on phones.

front: Repurpose content for use in multiple platforms
back: Repurposing content means adapting one piece of content for several platforms, such as turning a blog post into social posts, a video, an infographic and an email. It saves time and reaches more people.

front: Explain the impact of digital techniques on public relations practices
back: Digital techniques have changed PR through instant news cycles, social media monitoring, online newsrooms, influencer relations, direct communication with the public and analytics that measure the impact of PR efforts.

front: Leverage social networks for customer engagement
back: Leveraging social networks for engagement means encouraging conversation through questions, polls, contests, user-generated content, live videos and quick responses to comments, building a community around the brand.

front: Implement digital marketing campaign
back: Implementing a digital campaign means launching planned content and ads across chosen channels, managing budgets and schedules, monitoring performance in real time and adjusting targeting or content to improve results.

front: Explain the use of storytelling in marketing
back: Storytelling in marketing uses narratives, such as a customer's journey, a founder's story or a brand's mission, to create emotional connections, make messages memorable and show how products improve people's lives.

front: Maintain a consistent brand voice in social content
back: Maintaining a consistent brand voice means using the same personality, tone, vocabulary and values in all social content. Style guides help everyone who posts keep the brand recognizable and trustworthy.

front: Develop and package content for social distribution
back: Developing and packaging content for social distribution means creating content in formats suited to each platform (videos, images, carousels, stories), adding captions and hashtags and scheduling it for the best times.

front: Create promotional signage
back: Creating promotional signage means designing signs that attract attention and communicate quickly. Effective signs have a clear message, readable fonts from a distance, strong contrast, brand colors and a call to action.

front: Monitor user-generated content (UGC)
back: Monitoring user-generated content (UGC), such as customer reviews, photos and social posts, means tracking what people share about a brand, responding appropriately, removing harmful content where allowed and reusing positive content with permission.

front: Moderate social chats
back: Moderating social chats means guiding online conversations, such as live chats or comment threads, by welcoming participants, keeping discussion on topic, answering questions, enforcing community rules and handling negative comments professionally.

front: Implement strategies to grow social-media following
back: Strategies to grow a social media following include posting valuable content consistently, engaging with followers, using relevant hashtags, collaborating with influencers, running contests, cross-promoting on other channels and using targeted ads.

front: Explain the relationship between promotion and brand
back: Promotion and brand are closely linked: promotion communicates the brand's identity, promise and personality to customers. Consistent promotional messages build brand awareness and image, while the brand gives promotion a clear, recognizable focus.

front: Develop property fact book
back: A property fact book contains detailed information about a hotel for sales use, including room types and counts, rates, meeting space dimensions and capacities, food and beverage options, amenities, location, policies and contacts.

front: Prepare sales kit
back: A sales kit gives salespeople materials to present a property to clients, such as brochures, floor plans, menus, rate sheets, photos, testimonials, proposals and contract templates, often in both print and digital form.

front: Describe the use of design principles in menu development
back: Menu design principles include organizing items in logical sections, placing high-profit items in prime spots (such as the top right of a two-page menu), using boxes or icons to highlight items, readable fonts and layout that matches the restaurant's image.

front: Identify effective menu descriptions
back: Effective menu descriptions are accurate, appealing and concise. They describe key ingredients, preparation methods and flavors using vivid but honest words, and they note allergens or dietary information where helpful.

front: Explain the nature of effective nutritional disclosures
back: Effective nutritional disclosures give accurate, easy-to-find information such as calories, allergens and dietary symbols. Chain restaurants with 20 or more locations must post calories on menus under FDA rules and provide additional nutrition information on request.

front: Discuss the nature of digital marketing
back: Digital marketing uses online channels, such as websites, search engines, social media, email, mobile apps and digital ads, to reach and engage customers. It allows precise targeting, personalization and real-time measurement.

front: Explain ethical considerations in digital marketing
back: Ethical considerations in digital marketing include respecting privacy and getting consent for data, being honest in ads, disclosing sponsored content, avoiding manipulative design, protecting children and securing customer data.

front: Explain the nature of quality management
back: Quality management involves ensuring that products, services, and processes consistently meet established standards and customer expectations. It focuses on planning, monitoring, and improving performance to reduce defects and increase efficiency. Effective quality management enhances customer satisfaction and organizational reputation.

front: Describe the nature of quality management frameworks (e.g., Six Sigma, ITIL, CMMI)
back:
(QM:002) (SP) Quality management frameworks provide structured methods for improving processes and performance. For example:
Six Sigma focuses on reducing defects through data-driven analysis ITIL improves IT service management and operational efficiency CMMI enhances process maturity and organizational capability These frameworks promote consistency, efficiency, and measurable improvement

front: Discuss the need for continuous improvement of the quality process
back: Continuous improvement ensures that processes adapt to changing customer expectations, technology, and competition. Regular evaluation helps identify inefficiencies and opportunities for enhancement. Ongoing refinement supports long-term competitiveness and operational excellence.

front: Discuss ethical considerations in quality management
back: Ethical quality management requires honesty in reporting results, transparency about product standards, and accountability for defects. Organizations must avoid falsifying data or ignoring safety concerns. Upholding ethical standards protects customers and maintains trust.

front: Explain the role of ethics in risk management
back: Ethics in risk management requires honesty, transparency, and accountability when identifying and reporting risks. Organizations must avoid concealing threats, misrepresenting data, or prioritizing profit over safety. Ethical risk management protects stakeholders and maintains organizational credibility.

front: Describe the use of technology in risk management
back: Technology supports risk management through data analytics, monitoring systems, cybersecurity tools, and risk assessment software. These tools help identify patterns, predict potential threats, and improve response planning. Technology increases accuracy, speed, and proactive decision-making.

front: Discuss legal considerations affecting risk management
back:
Legal considerations include compliance with industry regulations, workplace safety laws, environmental standards, and financial reporting requirements. Organizations must assess legal liabilities and ensure risk strategies align with regulatory obligations.
Noncompliance can result in fines, lawsuits, and reputational damage.

front: Discuss the relationship between risk and business objectives
back: Risk and business objectives are linked because every goal involves some uncertainty. Pursuing growth or innovation often means accepting more risk. Businesses manage risk so it stays at a level that supports, rather than threatens, their objectives.

front: Develop a risk management program
back: A risk management program identifies, assesses and controls risks. Steps include identifying risks, analyzing their likelihood and impact, choosing strategies (avoid, reduce, transfer, retain), assigning responsibility, implementing controls and reviewing results regularly.

front: Discuss the relationship between risk management and business finance
back: Risk management and business finance are closely related. Financial decisions involve risk, such as borrowing, investing or extending credit, and managing risks like interest rate, currency and credit risk protects cash flow and company value.

front: Discuss the nature of risk measurement
back: Risk measurement quantifies risk so it can be managed. Methods include probability and impact estimates, standard deviation of returns, beta, value at risk (VaR), sensitivity analysis and scenario or stress testing.

front: Identify business risks
back: Business risks are events that could cause loss. They include economic risks (recessions), natural risks (storms), human risks (theft, errors), market risks (changing demand), legal risks (lawsuits) and technological risks (data breaches).

front: Discuss the nature of risk control (i.e., internal and external)
back: Risk control means reducing the likelihood or impact of losses. Internal controls are procedures within the business, such as approvals, separation of duties and audits. External controls come from outside, such as regulators, auditors, insurance and laws.

front: Explain ways to assess risk
back: Ways to assess risk include risk matrices that rate likelihood and impact, historical data, insurance and industry statistics, inspections, scenario analysis and expert opinions. Assessment helps prioritize which risks need action first.

front: Discuss the nature of enterprise risk management (ERM)
back: Enterprise risk management (ERM) is a company-wide approach to identifying, assessing and managing all types of risks together, rather than department by department. It links risk management to strategy and helps leaders decide how much risk to accept.

front: Identify financial risk factors associated with business contracts (e.g., ratio requirements, restricted transactions, financial report filing requirements)
back: Business contracts, such as loan agreements, can carry financial risks, including required ratios (such as minimum current ratio), restrictions on transactions (such as new debt or dividends) and reporting requirements. Violating them can trigger penalties or immediate repayment.

front: Monitor for breach of contract of non-performance related terms and conditions
back: Monitoring for breach of contract means regularly checking that all parties meet nonfinancial terms and conditions, such as delivery schedules, quality standards, reporting duties and confidentiality, and acting quickly when terms are not met.

front: Maintain contract compliance documentation
back: Maintaining contract compliance documentation means keeping organized records that prove the business is meeting contract terms, such as reports filed, ratios calculated, deliveries made and approvals obtained. Good documentation protects the business in disputes and audits.

front: Evaluate alternative revenue arrangements (e.g., cost-plus pricing, contingent fees)
back: Alternative revenue arrangements include cost-plus pricing (cost plus an agreed markup), fixed-price contracts, contingent fees (paid only if a result is achieved) and time-and-materials billing. Each shifts risk differently between the business and its client.

front: Establish monitoring programs for contract-specific revenue arrangements
back: Monitoring programs for contract-specific revenue track whether revenue is earned and recorded according to each contract's terms. They include milestone tracking, cost tracking for cost-plus contracts, regular reviews and alerts for deadlines or overruns.

front: Develop monitoring programs for restrictive contract requirements
back: Monitoring programs for restrictive contract requirements track compliance with limits in agreements, such as restrictions on additional borrowing, asset sales or dividends. They use checklists, reviews and alerts before any restricted action is taken.

front: Establish processes for timely reporting of required information
back: Processes for timely reporting ensure required information reaches lenders, regulators and contract partners on schedule. They include reporting calendars, assigned responsibilities, standard templates, review and approval steps and reminders before deadlines.

front: Describe types of financial risks (e.g., interest rate risk, equity risk, commodity risk, etc.)
back: Types of financial risk include interest rate risk (changing rates), equity risk (stock price changes), commodity risk (raw material prices), currency risk (exchange rates), credit risk (borrowers not paying) and liquidity risk (not having cash when needed).

front: Describe types of indicators used to manage business risk (e.g., key risk indicators, key performance indicators, key process indicators)
back: Indicators used to manage risk include key risk indicators (KRIs), which warn of rising risk; key performance indicators (KPIs), which measure progress toward goals; and key process indicators, which track how well specific processes are working.

front: Describe international considerations affecting risk management
back: International risk management must account for political instability, currency fluctuations, trade regulations, cultural differences, and varying legal systems. Global operations increase exposure to economic and geopolitical risks. Effective planning helps organizations adapt to international uncertainties and protect global assets.

front: Assess business risks
back: Assessing business risks means estimating how likely each risk is and how much harm it could cause. Risks with high likelihood and high impact get the most attention. The assessment guides decisions to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept each risk.

front: Process special orders for retail sales
back: Processing a retail special order means recording the customer's exact request, checking availability and cost, collecting a deposit if required, placing the order, giving the customer an expected date and notifying them when it arrives.

front: Sell gift certificates
back: Selling gift certificates or cards involves explaining options and terms, processing payment, activating the card or issuing the certificate, recording the sale accurately and following laws about expiration dates and fees.

front: Explain the nature and scope of the selling function
back: Selling is the personal or impersonal process of helping customers satisfy needs through the purchase of goods or services. Its scope includes prospecting, approaching customers, determining needs, presenting products, answering objections, closing sales and following up.

front: Explain the use of brand names in selling
back: Brand names help in selling because customers recognize and trust them. Salespeople use brand reputation, quality and image to reassure customers, justify prices and build confidence in the purchase.

front: Arrange delivery of purchases
back: Arranging delivery means confirming the customer's address, delivery date and time, any setup needed and delivery charges, scheduling with the delivery team and giving the customer a confirmation.

front: Explain the selling process
back: The selling process includes prospecting, the pre-approach (preparation), approaching the customer, determining needs, presenting the product, handling objections, closing the sale and following up. Each step builds toward a satisfied customer.

front: Acquire product information for use in selling
back: Salespeople acquire product information from manufacturers' materials, training sessions, product labels, websites, trade publications, using the product themselves and customer feedback. Strong product knowledge builds confidence and credibility.

front: Explain the role of customer service as a component of selling relationships
back: Customer service supports selling relationships by building trust and satisfaction after the sale. Helpful service, such as answering questions, handling problems and following up, creates repeat business and referrals.

front: Explain legal and ethical considerations in selling
back: Legal considerations in selling include avoiding misrepresentation, honoring warranties, following contract law, cooling-off rules, consumer protection laws and avoiding bribery or price discrimination. Ethically, salespeople should be honest, avoid high-pressure tactics and put customers' needs first.

front: Describe the use of technology in the selling function
back: Technology in selling includes CRM software, mobile devices and tablets for presentations, video calls, email and social selling, e-commerce sites, point-of-sale systems and sales analytics that track leads and performance.

front: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits
back: Analyzing product information means identifying features (characteristics of the product, such as a 12-hour battery) and translating them into benefits (what the feature does for the customer, such as working all day without charging). Benefits drive buying decisions.

front: Establish relationship with customer/client
back: Establishing a relationship with a customer starts with a friendly greeting and approach, showing genuine interest, listening and being helpful rather than pushy. Trust built early leads to sales and repeat business.

front: Determine customer/client needs
back: Determining customer needs means asking open-ended questions, listening actively, observing the customer and confirming understanding, so the salesperson can recommend products that truly fit.

front: Differentiate between consumer and organizational buying behavior
back: Consumer buying involves individuals buying for personal use, often quickly and emotionally. Organizational buying involves businesses buying for operations or resale; purchases are larger, involve several decision-makers, follow formal processes and focus on value and relationships.

front: Recommend specific products
back: Recommending specific products means suggesting items that match the customer's stated needs, explaining how features provide benefits and offering a few good choices rather than overwhelming the customer.

front: Calculate miscellaneous charges for retail sales
back: Miscellaneous charges in retail sales include sales tax, delivery fees, installation, alterations, gift wrapping, layaway fees and extended warranties. Salespeople must calculate them correctly and explain them to customers.

front: Process retail sales documentation
back: Retail sales documentation includes sales receipts, invoices, special order forms, layaway agreements, credit slips and return forms. Processing it accurately ensures correct records, inventory updates and customer service.

front: Process complimentary offers and coupons/discounts
back: Processing complimentary offers, coupons and discounts means verifying that they are valid, applying them correctly in the register or system, following company policy and recording them accurately so sales and promotions can be tracked.

front: Accept checks from customers
back: Accepting checks means following store policy: verifying the date, amount, signature and payee, checking identification, using check verification services if available and recording required information.

front: Operate register/terminal
back: Operating a register or terminal means signing in, scanning or entering items, applying discounts and coupons, calculating totals, accepting payment, giving correct change and receipts and following security procedures.

front: Process returns/exchanges
back: Processing returns and exchanges means checking the receipt and the item's condition, following store policy, issuing a refund, exchange or store credit and recording the transaction so inventory is updated.

front: Explain factors that motivate people to choose a hospitality and tourism site
back: People choose hospitality and tourism sites based on price, location, reputation and reviews, amenities, quality of service, brand loyalty, recommendations, the purpose of the trip and the experiences or attractions available.

front: Recommend hospitality and tourism services
back: Recommending services means suggesting options that fit a guest's needs, such as a room type, dish, tour or package. Staff ask questions, listen to preferences, explain benefits and offer choices that improve the guest's experience.

front: Process sales transactions (e.g., cash, credit, check)
back: Processing sales transactions means accepting payment by cash, credit or debit card, mobile payment or check; entering the sale correctly; giving correct change or receipts; and following procedures for verification and security.

front: Pitch marketing communications idea to client
back: Pitching a marketing communications idea means presenting the concept to a client persuasively: explaining how it solves their problem, showing creative examples, supporting it with research and asking for approval.

front: Discuss motivational theories that impact buying behavior
back: Motivational theories explain why people buy. Maslow's hierarchy of needs suggests people buy to satisfy needs ranging from physical survival and safety to belonging, esteem and self-actualization. Rational, emotional and patronage motives also influence purchases.

front: Acquire knowledge of client's products/brands
back: Acquiring knowledge of a client's products and brands means studying their offerings, target market, competitors, brand identity and past marketing. Deep knowledge leads to better ideas and stronger client relationships.

front: Demonstrate good/service
back: Demonstrating a good or service means showing how it works and how it benefits the customer, letting the customer try it when possible and appealing to the senses to build interest and confidence.

front: Explain the nature of key account management
back: Key account management focuses on a business's most important customers. Key account managers build long-term relationships, understand clients' goals, coordinate service across departments and develop customized solutions to grow the account.

front: Monitor on-floor selling activities
back: Monitoring on-floor selling activities means observing salespeople, tracking sales against goals, making sure customers are greeted and helped, coaching staff and adjusting coverage during busy times.

front: Present an advertising campaign to clients
back: Presenting an advertising campaign means showing the client the strategy, creative work, media plan, budget and expected results. Effective presenters connect each element to the client's goals and handle questions confidently.

front: Provide information about incoming merchandise to sales staff
back: Providing information about incoming merchandise means telling sales staff what new products are arriving, when, their features, prices and promotions, so they can answer questions and sell them effectively.

front: Provide service after the sale
back: Providing service after the sale includes following up, answering questions, handling problems, providing support and asking for feedback. It builds satisfaction, repeat business and referrals.

front: Up-sell to enhance customer experience
back: Up-selling means suggesting a higher-priced or additional item that improves the guest's experience, such as a room upgrade, dessert or premium tour. It increases sales and satisfaction when the suggestion truly fits the guest's needs.

front: Process telephone orders in hospitality and tourism
back: Processing telephone orders involves answering promptly and politely, taking down details accurately, repeating the order back, noting special requests, quoting prices and times, collecting payment information securely and confirming the order.

front: Process special orders in hospitality and tourism
